# Craters named for physicists and chemists

20 articles

## Arrhenius (Martian crater)

Arrhenius is a roughly 129-km-wide impact crater in the southern hemisphere of Mars, centered near 39.97°S, 122.6°E, named for Swedish physical chemist Svante Arrhenius and IAU-approved in 1973.

## Barth (Martian crater)

Barth is an impact crater on Mars, 111 kilometers wide in the Arabia Terra region, named in 2019 for American atmospheric physicist Charles A. Barth.

## Bouguer (Martian crater)

Bouguer is a 107.78-km-diameter impact crater on Mars at 18.46°S, 27.27°E, named in 1973 for French physicist-hydrographer Pierre Bouguer (1698-1758) and cataloged by the USGS/IAU Gazetteer.

## Coblentz (Martian crater)

Coblentz, a 101.75-km impact crater on Mars at 54.9S, 269.69E, named for William W. Coblentz and IAU-approved in 1973; Gazetteer Feature ID 1257.

## Curie (Martian crater)

Curie crater, Mars: IAU-approved 114.10-km impact crater at 28.81°N, 355.20°E (Feature ID 1351), named for physicist Pierre Curie under the large-crater scientist naming rule; studied via Viking IRTM thermal inertia.

## Heaviside (Martian crater)

Heaviside is an 83.28-km-diameter impact crater on Mars at 70.50°S, 264.78°E in the southern cratered highlands, named for British physicist Oliver Heaviside (1850–1925) and approved by the IAU in 1973.

## Helmholtz (Martian crater)

Helmholtz is a large impact crater in the southern highlands of Mars, named after the German physicist Hermann von Helmholtz. It was adopted by the IAU in 1973.

## Hooke (Martian crater)

Hooke is a 139 km impact crater on Mars at 44.86°S, 315.60°E, near the northern edge of the Argyre basin. It contains two nested impact structures, dunes, yardangs, and seasonal carbon dioxide frost, and is named for Robert Hooke.

## Huxley (Martian crater)

Huxley is a 107-km-wide IAU-approved impact crater on Mars at 62.67°S, 100.77°E, named for British biologist Thomas Henry Huxley and approved in 1973; a smaller lunar crater shares the name.

## Lederberg (Martian crater)

Lederberg is a Martian impact crater, 87.25 km in diameter. Located in the Xanthe Terra region, it was adopted in 2012 to honor American molecular biologist Joshua Leder.

## Martz (Martian crater)

Martz is a ~97 km diameter impact crater in Terra Cimmeria, Mars, at about 35 degrees south latitude, named in 1973 for American physicist Edwin P. Martz and known for its 1,500 m central peak with gullies.

## Mie (Martian crater)

Mie is a 104-km-diameter impact crater on Mars at 48.16°N, 139.65°E, IAU-approved in 1973 and named for German physicist Gustav Mie (1868-1957); studied for secondary deposits and subsurface volatiles.

## Pasteur (Martian crater)

Pasteur crater on Mars, 116.15 km wide at 19.31N 24.62E in eastern Arabia Terra, IAU-named 1973 for Louis Pasteur; layered sedimentary floor deposits and actively moving barchan dunes. Distinct from the 232.77 km lunar crater Pasteur.

## Ramanathan (Martian crater)

Ramanathan is a Martian impact crater, 89.00 km in diameter, located in north-central Arabia. It was named for Indian physicist Kalpathy Ramakrishna Ramanathan in 2022.

## Reynolds (Martian crater)

Reynolds crater, a 90.69-km impact crater on Mars at 74.99°S, 202.41°E, IAU-named in 1973 for British physicist Osborne Reynolds (1842–1912), cataloged in the USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.

## Rutherford (Martian crater)

Rutherford is an IAU-named impact crater on Mars in Arabia Terra, about 107-110 km across, centered near 19 degrees north latitude. Named for physicist Ernest Rutherford in 1973, its floor shows basaltic sand and a dark wind streak.

## Stoney (Martian crater)

Stoney, Martian crater, IAU-approved 1973, named for physicist George Johnstone Stoney; 161.37 km diameter at 69.61°S, 221.49°E in Mars's cratered southern highlands.

## Tyndall (Martian crater)

Tyndall is an 83 km impact crater on Mars at 39.73°N, 169.97°E in western Arcadia Planitia, named for British physicist John Tyndall and approved by the IAU in 1973.

## Wallace (Martian crater)

Wallace is a 110.90-km-diameter impact crater on Mars at 170.78°E, 52.48°S, officially named in 1973 by the IAU for Alfred Russel Wallace, the British biologist who argued in Is Mars Habitable? (1907) that Mars was not habitable.

## Wien (Martian crater)

Wien is a 115.14 km impact crater on Mars at 10.57°S, 139.75°E, approved by the IAU in 1976 and named for Wilhelm Wien, the German physicist (1864–1928).

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter H – N *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

This is a partial [list of craters on Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"). There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here only contains named Martian craters starting with the letter A – G *(see also lists for [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N") and [O – Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_O–Z "List of craters on Mars: O–Z"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

There are hundreds of thousands of [impact craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars"), but only some of them have names. This list here contains only named Martian craters starting with the letter O – Z *(see also lists for [A – G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_A–G "List of craters on Mars: A–G") and [H – N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars:_H–N "List of craters on Mars: H–N"))*.

Large Martian craters (greater than 60 kilometers in diameter) are named after famous scientists and [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") authors; smaller ones (less than 60 km in diameter) get their names from towns on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). Craters cannot be named for living people, and small crater names are not intended to be commemorative – that is, a small crater isn't actually named after a specific town on Earth, but rather its name comes at random from a pool of terrestrial place names, with some exceptions made for craters near landing sites.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-2) Latitude and longitude are given as planetographic coordinates with west longitude.

# Curie (Martian crater)

**Curie** is an impact crater on Mars, centered at 28.81° north latitude and 355.20° east longitude in the northern hemisphere of the planet, with a diameter of 114.10 kilometers as recorded in the Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature.[1](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/1351) It carries the name of the physicist [Pierre Curie](/pierre-curie), following the International Astronomical Union convention that large Martian craters be named for famous scientists.[2](https://planetologia.elte.hu/ipcd/vaucouleurs.pdf) • [3](https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/why-and-how-nasa-gives-a-name-to-every-spot-it-studies-on-mars-2/)

## Naming

Official names on Mars are approved by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) and recorded in the Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, which the USGS Astrogeology Science Center maintains in cooperation with the IAU's Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature.[3](https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/why-and-how-nasa-gives-a-name-to-every-spot-it-studies-on-mars-2/) • [4](https://www.usgs.gov/tools/gazetteer-planetary-nomenclature) The naming convention places Curie in the large-crater category: craters larger than 37 miles (60 kilometers) are named for famous scientists or science-fiction authors, while smaller craters take the names of towns with populations under 100,000 people.[3](https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/why-and-how-nasa-gives-a-name-to-every-spot-it-studies-on-mars-2/) At 114.10 km across, Curie falls well above that threshold.[1](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/1351)

The IAU's compiled list of large crater names on Mars records the namesake as "Curie, P.", that is, the French physicist Pierre Curie (1859–1906).[2](https://planetologia.elte.hu/ipcd/vaucouleurs.pdf) The Curie family name appears across the solar system's naming schemes in related forms: on Mars, the nearby-named [Becquerel](/becquerel) crater honors [Henri Becquerel](/henri-becquerel), who shared the 1903 [Nobel Prize in Physics](/nobel-prize-in-physics) with Marie and Pierre Curie for the discovery of radioactivity.[6](https://www.esa.int/About_Us/ESAC/A_radiating_beauty_on_Mars)

## Location and setting

The Gazetteer places the crater's center at 28.81°N, 355.20°E in the planetocentric, east-positive coordinate system, with an alternative listing at 4.80° west longitude; its rim spans latitudes from about 27.82° to 29.71°N.[1](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/1351) This puts it in the cratered terrain of Mars' northern hemisphere, in the general region of western [Arabia Terra](/arabia-terra). A thermal inertia study of the crater noted a general southeastern trend toward lower thermal inertia values in the surrounding study region, a trend the authors suggested may be related to the proximity of the Arabia region, mainly to the south and east of Curie.[5](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19870014076)

## Physical characteristics

The crater is a complex impact structure. The NASA thermal inertia report describes a region near the central peak on the crater floor, with material also visible on the crater walls.[5](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19870014076) Central peaks form in large impact craters when the excavated cavity rebounds during the modification stage of crater formation, and on Mars a higher percentage of relatively unmodified craters below about 30 km diameter show central peaks than on the Moon, a difference attributed to Mars' gravity field.[7](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0019103576901275)

Thermal inertia, the measure of how well surface material holds onto heat, distinguishes fine sand, which releases heat quickly, from large particles such as boulders, which hold heat longer.[8](https://doi.org/10.1029/2020JE006801) Measurements of this kind from the Viking IRTM instrument were used to characterize the surface materials in and around Curie.[5](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19870014076)

## Observations by Mars orbiters

Curie has appeared in orbiter-based studies of Martian surface processes. A survey of western Arabia Terra craters and their dark wind streaks, using Mars Global Surveyor Mars Orbiter Camera images from 1997 to 2001, noted that some dark material on crater floors in western Arabia Terra is not dune field material and is not like the dark surfaces in Curie Crater, using Curie as a comparison point for the region's varied dark deposits.[9](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2001JE001587)

More broadly, the crater sits within the part of Mars that retains the planet's most complete record of impact cratering; fresh Martian craters are commonly surrounded by layered or lobate ejecta morphologies unlike the radial patterns seen around fresh craters on the Moon and Mercury, a difference linked to subsurface volatiles in the target material.[10](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2002JE002036)
